children: Sashidhar Jagdishan's tenure as managing director and chief executive of HDFC Bank will likely be remembered as one of the most consequential periods in the lender's history.

He steered the bank through the Covid-19 pandemic, completed the transformational merger with HDFC Ltd and oversaw the listing of HDB Financial Services. But the period also brought significant challenges, with the enlarged balance sheet putting pressure on funding, margins and returns.

Brokerages broadly agree that Jagdishan leaves behind an exceptionally strong banking franchise. The more difficult question, however, is whether the next chief executive can restore the profitability metrics and growth profile investors had come to associate with HDFC Bank.
A difficult backdrop

ICICI Securities said Jagdishan's tenure included some of the bank's most important strategic milestones, including the merger with HDFC Ltd and the listing of HDB Financial Services. But the brokerage also pointed to a series of regulatory and governance issues that attracted investor attention during the period.
The brokerage's broader assessment is that the leadership change comes at a particularly important point for the bank.

While the succession process itself creates uncertainty, ICICI Securities believes the incoming CEO will also have to confront some difficult strategic decisions around the structure of the balance sheet.
"The new MD&CEO could prioritise fixing the balance sheet structure, even at the cost of near-term growth," the brokerage said.
That challenge has become more prominent following the HDFC Ltd merger.

ICICI Securities noted that the bank had seen a significant decline in its CASA ratio as a proportion of external funding following the merger. At the same time, an increase in the cost of funds and moderation in lending yields had created pressure on medium-term profitable growth.
The merger's impact on returns
The merger transformed HDFC Bank's scale, but brokerages say the larger balance sheet has also created a more complicated operating environment.

Macquarie said the bank's return on assets remained between 1.8% and 2% through FY21-24, before declining to around 1.7-1.8% in FY25-26. The decline reflected the larger balance sheet, increased funding intensity and pressure on margins following the merger.

However, the brokerage argued that this should not be seen as evidence of franchise impairment, describing Jagdishan's record instead as one of "considerable execution against an unusually difficult backdrop."
Axis Capital struck a similar note, saying the bank's sheer size and intense competition among large lenders could continue to weigh on the expansion of its return ratios.
The brokerage expects near-term return on equity to remain around 14%, warning that any meaningful transformation would take time.

Axis Capital said that while Jagdishan's decision not to seek another term had removed uncertainty around the length of his tenure, the focus would now shift to the successor and the strategic choices made by the new leadership.
"Smooth transition and new CEO's strategic choices will be key to any meaningful re-rating," the brokerage said.
A new CEO, and potentially a new strategy
For Jefferies, the leadership transition comes after a difficult period for the stock but also at a point when valuations have become significantly more attractive.

The brokerage said the new CEO would have to address concerns around the bank's funding profile and the possibility of senior-management churn during the transition. It also flagged the uncertainty surrounding succession as a potential drag on earnings and valuations.
Jefferies nevertheless argued that after the stock's sharp decline, the risk-reward had become more balanced.

ICICI Securities, meanwhile, believes the extent of HDFC Bank's eventual re-rating could depend heavily on the "course correction" undertaken by the new CEO. The brokerage said a large part of the stock's weakness appeared to be priced in after its significant underperformance against the banking index over the past three years.
The crown of thorns
The immediate market focus will inevitably be on who succeeds Jagdishan.
But brokerages suggest the bigger issue is what the successor does after taking charge.

The next CEO will inherit one of India's strongest banking franchises and an institution with enormous scale. But that scale has come with a more demanding balance-sheet structure, higher funding requirements and pressure on returns.

ICICI Securities believes fixing the funding and balance-sheet structure could require sacrificing some near-term growth. Axis Capital sees strategic choices by the incoming CEO as critical to any meaningful re-rating. And Jefferies believes the transition itself could weigh on earnings and valuations until the market has greater clarity.

title: Merger to margins: How brokerages assess Sashidhar Jagdishan's tenure at HDFC Bank
